newsitem.title: JAPAN: POLL-Japan economy enters phase of plodding growth.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Japan economy enters phase of plodding growth.

text.p: Japan's economy is gaining strength bit by bit, with the growth rate set to rise to between two and three percent in the next business year, a Reuters poll of economists showed on Thursday.
While there was disagreement over how soon the recovery would settle into a virtuous business cycle, most economists agreed the economy was entering a phase of plodding, unspectacular growth.

Thirty-seven economists produced a mean average prediction of 1.7 percent growth in real gross domestic product (GDP) for this business year, unchanged from the previous survey in April. The range, however, narrowed, with a low of 1.1 percent growth and a high of 3.4 percent.
Forecasts from 26 of the economists for the 1998/99 business year produced an average of 2.5 percent growth, slightly below the previous survey's average of 2.7 percent.

Earlier fears that government attempts to rein in spending would severely dampen growth, in particular through the raising of the nation's sales tax to five percent from three percent in April, had largely waned.

"The economy is not too bad. There are obviously some risks, for example, if they've overdone it on fiscal tightening, but I don't think that's too high a possibility," said Richard Jerram, an economist at ING Baring Securities.
A boom in exports, on the back of a healthy U.S. economy, helped to offset a decline in consumer spending during the April to June period.

Exports are expected to lend a large dose of support to growth, although some economists caution that the manufacturing sector represents less than a quarter of the economy and its trickle-down effect can only go so far.
Capital expenditure and to a lesser extent a recovery in consumer spending were seen as the key engines of growth.
While economists differed on the precise strength of the recovery in consumer spending, many saw support from wage increases on the back of improved corporate profits.
But most were upbeat on business investment plans.

Although telecommunications-related spending should drop a notch, investment in increased capacity and spending on new machinery should rise, said Shuji Shirota, an economist at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics.

Yamaichi Research predicts a 5.3 percent rise in capital expenditure this business year and a seven percent rise in 1998/99, while GDP growth rates were projected at 1.8 and 2.3 percent respectively for those years.

Economists also noted the growing polarisation between the big export-oriented manufacturers and their poorer cousins -- non-manufacturers and small to medium sized companies -- but said that some widening of the gap was unavoidable.

"The economy is still going to recover, even though some firms will get left behind. There is still some sand in this mechanism of a virtuous cycle," said Matthew Poggi, an economist at Lehman Brothers.
Some saw export profits slowly but surely working their way through the system to narrow the gap between large and small firms.
But others said that, although the economy should improve overall, the gap between those doing well and those not doing so well was unlikely to shrink.
The survey was conducted from July 7 to July 9.
